column2: Thermal camera. The glass is a thermal imager's live view in an honest false-colour palette (ironbow: black-violet cold, through magenta and orange, to yellow-white hot), with the camera's own flat overlay: a crosshair spot meter with a live temperature readout, the colour scale bar with min/max, a mode label, all in a small instrument font you draw. The time is made of warm things, each digit one or a few objects whose heat pattern makes the numeral (a 0 a steaming mug's rim seen from above, a 1 a candle with its flame, an 8 a sleeping cat curled in two loops, a 7 a hot clothes iron and its cord, a 3 two coils of a hair straightener...), so the image is flat heat, not drawn outlines: soft-edged hot cores, cooler surroundings, heat bleeding into the cold background. Always alive at 60 fps: steam and hot air plumes drift up as warm wisps, the cat breathes, a candle flame flickers, the spot meter hunts between hot points and its number changes. Minute turn: the old digit's object cools (its colours slide down the palette to the background, gone before :00), then the new one warms up from its hottest point outward (after :00); the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the camera cycles palettes (ironbow, rainbow, white-hot, black-hot, arctic) in scan wipes, or someone's hand-print is left and fades. Keep the palette honest and flat: heat maps through a lookup table, no shading.

The Bayeux Tapestry. The 2:1 strip is a band of embroidered linen in the tapestry's eight wool colours (terracotta, ochre yellow, sage and dark green, two blues, near-black), with its upper and lower border friezes of beasts and the Latin inscription running along the top. The numerals are figures and things in the tapestry's flat stitched style: laid-and-couched work in solid colour fields, stem-stitch outlines, embroidered on visible linen weave: Norman ships with dragon prows, horses with riders, towers, trees, so each digit is a scene element shaped as the numeral (a 1 a tower, a 2 a horse with an arched neck, a 0 a ship's round shield ring, a 4 a mast and sail...), designed as a set that reads. The scroll pans slowly and continuously along the strip (the tapestry is 70 m long) with figures in the friezes and between the digits walking, rowing, feasting. Minute turn: a needle with wool thread unpicks the old digit's stitches (thread pulling out in lines, gone before :00) and stitches in the new one (laid threads first, then couching, then the outline), after :00. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. Halley's comet streaks across (as in the tapestry), or a whole new section scrolls in with a cavalry charge. Inscription in a stitched Romanesque capital alphabet you draw ("HIC HORA X" etc.). Flat colour, stitch texture only.

Greek black-figure vase painting. The glass is the frieze band of an amphora: warm terracotta-orange clay with figures painted in glossy black slip, details incised as thin lines of bare clay, a few touches of added red and white, meander (Greek key) borders top and bottom. The numerals are black-figure athletes and heroes in profile: runners, discus throwers, wrestlers, a warrior with a round shield and spear, Herakles with the lion, dancers, horses; each digit is one or two figures whose bodies, limbs, shields and spears make the digit (a 0 the round hoplite shield, a 1 a spear-bearer, a 7 a javelin thrower mid-throw, a 4 a wrestler hold, an 8 two shields stacked...). Design all ten as a set that reads first as digits. Always alive at 60 fps: the vase turns slowly, so the frieze scrolls past (flat scroll, no 3D wrap), figures run in place in the classical running pose, a meander border slides, an owl blinks. Minute turn: the old figure runs off along the frieze and a new figure runs in to strike the new digit's pose (or the painter's brush paints it in black slip, then the incision lines are scratched in). Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a chariot race or a procession crosses the frieze, or the vase flips to red-figure technique (figures in reserved clay on a black ground) for the hour's start. Strictly flat: black slip, clay, incision lines; no shading.

The blueprint. A Prussian-blue cyanotype sheet with white lines: an architect's or engineer's drawing, with the grid, title block, border, scale bar and handwritten notes in a technical lettering you draw. The numerals are drafted objects shown in plan and section: building floor plans whose walls make the digits (doors as arcs, windows as triple lines, stairs as hatched treads), or machine parts in orthographic view with centre lines, hatching for cut material, dimension lines with arrowheads and numbers. Design all ten digits as a set of drawings that read first as digits. Always alive at 60 fps: a drafting machine or T-square and set square slide over the sheet, a compass draws an arc, dimension lines extend, a cursor of a plotter pen moves, revision clouds appear and vanish, the paper's chalky grain. Minute turn: the old digit is erased (eraser rubs, crumbs, faint ghost) before :00, and the new one is drafted after :00: construction lines first in faint blue-white, then hard object lines inked over, then hatching, then dimensions. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a new sheet is laid down (revision letter goes up, the title block updates), or the drawing flips from plan to elevation. Strictly flat line drawing: line weights, hatching and white on blue; no shading.

The kilim. A flat-woven rug on the loom, which is native to this pixel grid: every pixel a weft pass, in a small palette of natural dyes (madder red, indigo, walnut brown, weld yellow, undyed ivory, a touch of green), with the diagonal-stepped motifs, hooks, ram's horns, latch hooks and borders of Anatolian kilims. The numerals are woven into the field as motifs: each digit built from the kilim's own stepped diagonals and hooked ornaments, with slit-weave gaps where colours meet vertically, as real kilims have; design all ten so they read first as digits. Always alive at 60 fps: the weft shimmers, a weaver's shuttle and beater move along the top edge, tassels or fringe sway at the ends, the warp threads show between passes. Minute turn: the loom weaves the new digit: the old part of the rug rolls up onto the beam at the top (or the weaver unpicks rows), and the shuttle passes row by row building the new numeral line by line from the bottom, each pass a visible thread sliding across; the time is never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the whole rug is cut off the loom and a new one begins in a new colour scheme, or the rug is shaken out and lands with the new hour. Strictly flat: woven pixels and weave texture, no shading.

Pop-art comic panel (Lichtenstein / 1960s comics). Ben-Day dot fields in cyan, magenta and yellow, thick black ink outlines, flat primaries, speech balloons and onomatopoeia lettering. The numerals are comic objects and lettering in that style: big inked block numerals in a hand-lettered comic style you draw, filled with Ben-Day dots and colour, with action lines, inside a comic panel with gutters. A small cast acts in panels around them: a pilot in a jet cockpit, a crying girl with a tear (as in the famous paintings), a ray gun, a phone; with captions ("MEANWHILE, AT TEN O'NINE..."). Always alive at 60 fps: Ben-Day dots shimmer with misregistration, speed lines stream, the cast blinks and moves in flat cel animation, a speech balloon's text types out. Minute turn: a comic action takes the old digit out (a fist, a "POW!" burst, a jet's "WHAAM!" in a starburst, the digit shatters as flat shards) before :00, and the new digit slams in with a "KA-CHUNK" after :00. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the panel layout rearranges (gutters slide, a page turn, a splash page) with the time readable. Strictly flat: dots, outlines, primaries; no gradients or shading.

The antique sea chart. A hand-coloured copperplate nautical chart on aged paper: coastlines with hachured shores, rhumb lines radiating from a compass rose, depth soundings as tiny numbers, a cartouche with a title in a copperplate script you draw, sea monsters and ships drawn in engraved line with flat watercolour washes (pale blue sea edge, ochre land, pink borders). The numerals are islands and coastlines: each digit an island or archipelago whose coast traces the numeral, with engraved hachure along the shore, a few hills drawn as profile bumps, a harbour, all flat line and wash. Always alive at 60 fps: a little ship sails a dotted route between the digits, its wake drawn as trailing engraved lines, a sea serpent coils in and out of the water, the compass rose's needle swings, a whale spouts. Minute turn: the cartographer's quill redraws the coast: the old island is scraped/washed away into blank sea (gone before :00) and the new coastline is inked stroke by stroke, then the wash is laid in (after :00); time never wrong. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. a storm sweeps across in engraved wind-heads blowing, or the chart is rolled and a new sheet unrolled. Strictly flat: engraving lines and flat washes, no shading.

Matisse's cut-outs (the late gouache-painted paper works: Jazz, The Snail, Blue Nudes, Icarus). The glass is a wall of flat, saturated painted-paper shapes pinned up on white or coloured paper grounds: organic leaves and seaweed fronds, stars, waves, coral, birds, the blue figure. The numerals are cut from painted paper in Matisse's hand: scissor-cut organic edges (not geometric fonts), slightly wobbly, flat colour with a faint gouache brush texture and tiny pin heads, designed as a set of ten that read first as digits, each in a different saturated colour against contrasting grounds (ultramarine, lemon, vermilion, emerald, magenta, black). Always alive at 60 fps: the cut shapes sway as if in a draught (flat rotations of a few degrees about their pins, not 3D), leaves flutter, a cut star twinkles by swapping shapes, a paper bird crosses, colour fields slowly shift. Minute turn: a pair of scissors cuts the new digit out of a painted sheet along its contour (the snipping blades and the paper curling as a flat strip), the old digit is unpinned and drops away (before :00), the new one is pinned up (after :00). Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the whole composition rearranges into "The Snail"'s spiral of coloured squares and back, with the time readable. Strictly flat: painted paper, no shading.
